$comment: Browser registry for the memory benchmark. Adding a browser is a JSON edit,
not a code change, as long as it belongs to one of the launch families in
lib/launch.js (chromium | gecko | blanc).
bundlePath and executableName accept a string or an array of candidates;
the first combination that exists on disk wins. Vendors rename their
bundles between releases (Zen shipped as both 'Zen Browser.app' and
'Zen.app'), so candidates are cheaper than a support ticket.
Candidates are for a bundle the vendor RENAMED, never for release channels:
resolution takes the first that exists and the row is labelled from the
entry, so a nightly listed alongside a stable bundle would publish under
the stable label. A separate channel gets a separate id.
extraBlankTabs records tabs a browser opens on its own beyond the workload
URLs, so the report can disclose the real tab count. The per-page column
divides by workload pages regardless, so this never flatters a browser.
blockingClass drives the report's grouping: none | trackers | ads+trackers.
It is NOT cosmetic. A browser that blocks ads renders less content, so
ranking it against a non-blocking browser in one column would present a
product difference as an engine-efficiency result. Any entry whose class is
uncertain must say so in notes and be confirmed on the first real run —
these defaults change between vendor releases and none of them have been
verified on a real machine yet.

browsers.label: Blanc
notes: main.js creates one blanc://newtab at startup in addition to the URLs
passed on the command line — hence extraBlankTabs: 1.
Blanc CANCELS every http(s) main-frame request until its blocker is
compiled (installStartupNavigationGate, main.js:226/3751). On a cold
profile that gate can stay shut for the whole sampling window, so the
runner warms a template profile first and verifies every loaded cell
against the browser's own idle baseline.
Do NOT set BLANC_TEST=1 for a benchmark run: acceptanceTestMode in
main.js disables ad blocking, which would measure a configuration the
app never ships.

browsers.label: Blanc (blocking off)
notes: Isolates what the built-in blocker contributes. The runner seeds
settings.json in the throwaway profile with adblockEnabled: false.
Shares a bundle path with the 'blanc' entry, so a process surviving one
cell would be attributed to the other — which is why quit() reaps the
whole measured process set rather than just the root pid.

browsers.label: Google Chrome
notes: The report's reference row: percentages are relative to Chrome rather
than to whichever browser scored lowest.

browsers.label: Zen Browser
browsers.blocking: ETP Standard — tracker cookies, cryptominers, fingerprinters; does NOT block ads, and blocks tracking content only in private windows
notes: Zen ships its own onboarding, separate from Mozilla's about:welcome, so
browser.aboutwelcome.enabled=false does not touch it. Every cell mints a
fresh profile, so every Zen cell is a first run; its welcome flow hides
the browser content until a human clicks through, which would settle
fast and clean and be recorded as an excellent result at the requested
tab count. extraPrefs sets the pref that suppresses it — if a future
build renames it, the welcome screen returns silently and only the load
check against Zen's own idle baseline catches it.
CONFIRMED 2026-08-09 on Zen 1.x / macOS 27: user.js startup-homepage
tab seeding IS honoured — the upstream report of it failing on macOS
aarch64 (zen-browser/desktop#12154) did not reproduce here. But Zen
consumes the FIRST startup entry with its own workspace/new-tab
surface, so the first workload URL was silently dropped (9/10 pages,
twice, deterministically). geckoUserJs now leads with about:blank to
absorb that.

browsers.label: Zen Twilight (nightly)
browsers.blocking: ETP Standard — tracker cookies, cryptominers, fingerprinters; does NOT block ads, and blocks tracking content only in private windows
notes: Zen's nightly channel, which installs as Twilight.app with the same
'zen' executable. It exists as its own id so nobody 'fixes' a
Twilight-only machine by appending the bundle to the stable entry:
resolution takes the first candidate that exists and labels the row from
the entry, so that edit would publish a nightly under the label 'Zen
Browser'. Never cite this row as Zen.

browsers.label: Firefox
notes: Run alongside Zen: it separates what Zen's own changes cost from what
Gecko costs, which is the honest way to read a Zen result.

browsers.label: Brave
notes: Brave's updater (Sparkle) lives inside the app bundle and keeps its
check state in ~/Library/Preferences, which --user-data-dir does not
reset — so a fresh profile does not prevent an update check firing mid
measurement. --disable-brave-update suppresses it. This changes no
process-model knob, so it does not violate the no-flags rule; the Gecko
driver already sets app.update.auto=false for the same reason.
UNVERIFIED: whether Brave opens a welcome tab on a fresh profile despite
--no-first-run. If it does, extraBlankTabs must be raised.

browsers.label: Vivaldi
browsers.blocking: built-in blocker, trackers only at stock settings
notes: Vivaldi ships its blocker set to block trackers, NOT ads, out of the
box; the registry previously said 'built-in blocker (stock settings)',
which read as an ad-blocking peer and would have grouped it with Blanc
and Brave. UNVERIFIED against a real install — confirm in Settings >
Privacy before publishing, since a wrong class silently moves the row
into the wrong comparison group.
Vivaldi's own UI is a web page rendered in a renderer process, so its
process count and baseline include the browser chrome itself — the same
property Blanc has, and unlike Chrome's native UI.

browsers.label: Arc
notes: Arc manages its own profile/space model and may ignore --user-data-dir,
in which case the row would reflect the tester's real profile. This note
is surfaced in the report so it cannot be missed; verify with
--keep-profiles that the throwaway profile was actually populated.

browsers.label: LibreWolf
notes: The only entry whose blocking comes from a bundled extension, so the
report's 'no extensions' limit does not hold for this row and uBO's own
memory is inside its total.

browsers.label: Safari
unsupportedReason: Safari has no command-line profile isolation and no command-line tab
opening, so it cannot be measured on the same terms as the others: a
run would use the tester's real profile, with their extensions, their
history and their iCloud tabs. Driving it over AppleScript is possible
but the profile problem remains, so a Safari row would not be
comparable and is deliberately omitted rather than footnoted.

browsers.label: Orion
unsupportedReason: WebKit-based with no documented command-line profile or tab interface.
